analysis.one_liner: Legislates approval of the Keystone XL oil pipeline and declares environmental review complete.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 266-153 with 28 Democrats joining all voting Republicans, but the Senate never took a vote and the bill died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would shortcut the normal permitting process by having Congress directly approve the Keystone XL pipeline, a project to carry Canadian oil sands crude across the border to Gulf Coast refineries. It would declare the 2014 environmental review final and complete, waiving further review under national environmental and endangered species laws [S2][S4]. It would also channel all legal challenges to the D.C. federal appeals court [S2][S4]. The bill passed the House within days of being introduced but never received a vote in the Senate [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada, the Canadian company building the pipeline, would get what normal permitting had not yet granted: a statute approving its project. Oil sands producers would gain a new route to move crude. Pipeline construction would create temporary construction jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Congress would itself authorize TransCanada to build, connect, operate, and maintain the pipeline and cross-border facilities described in its 2012 application to the State Department [S2][S4].

The bill declares the January 2014 environmental impact statement as fully satisfying the National Environmental Policy Act and any required federal consultation or review, including under the Endangered Species Act, so no further environmental review would be needed [S2][S4].

It keeps any federal permits already issued in effect and concentrates all legal challenges in the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, sparing the project from drawn-out litigation in multiple courts [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Communities and waterways along the pipeline route would bear spill and leak risk without any further environmental review. Federal environmental and endangered species protections would be waived for this one project. Landowners along the route would still face the normal process for securing pipeline access across private property.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override the normal review process: no new environmental analysis, no endangered species consultation, and all court challenges funneled to a single friendly forum, leaving future problems with the pipeline harder to catch or fix [S2][S4].

Democrats' motion to send the bill back with a requirement that TransCanada contribute to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund the way conventional crude producers do was rejected 180-237, meaning oil sands crude would be treated differently for spill-cleanup funding [S6][S7].

The main economic benefit to the public — jobs and modest fuel price effects — is temporary, while spill and climate risks from oil sands crude are long-term; even supporters acknowledged most permanent jobs along the line are small in number.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go almost entirely to one company and the oil industry: a legislatively mandated approval plus a waiver of the environmental reviews any other project would face. The costs — spill risk on land and water the pipeline crosses, and a precedent for Congress to override environmental law project by project — fall on the public. There is no mechanism in the bill for the public to recapture value if fuel prices or jobs fall short of expectations.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 266-153 just three days after introduction, but the Senate only placed it on its calendar and never voted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 6, 2015, the bill was fast-tracked through a Rules Committee resolution the next day that waived points of order and allowed it to be considered as read [S6].

On January 9, 2015, a Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions requiring TransCanada to certify that oil sands products would be treated like conventional crude for Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund contributions failed 180-237, with all voting Republicans opposed and all voting Democrats in favor [S6][S7].
The House passed the bill the same day 266-153, with 238 of 242 voting Republicans in favor and 28 of 181 voting Democrats in favor [S8].

The Senate received the bill on January 12, 2015, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders, but it never received a Senate vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S6][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the pipeline came out ahead: the environmental reviews the bill would have waived were never overridden, and TransCanada never got the congressional approval it sought. Landowners and communities along the proposed route were spared a statute that would have limited their ability to challenge the project in court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline opponents and communities along the route

for.name: Rep. Kevin Cramer
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 2015, to approve the Keystone XL pipeline by statute.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.role: Majority-controlled committee that sets floor terms
for.what_they_did: Reported H. Res. 19 on January 7, one day after introduction, waiving all points of order and allowing the bill to be considered as read, moving it to a floor vote within three days.

for.name: 238 of 242 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage on January 9, 2015.

for.name: 28 of 181 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, joining Republicans to pass the bill 266-153.

against.name: 153 of 181 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage, and all 180 voting Democrats supported the motion to recommit requiring oil spill fund contributions.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Opposed congressional approval of Keystone XL and later vetoed the Senate's companion Keystone bill, making enactment of H.R. 3 unlikely; the Senate leadership instead moved its own version of the bill rather than take up the House-passed measure.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed H.R. 3 to the Senate floor; the Senate instead debated its own Keystone bill (S. 1), leaving H.R. 3 on the calendar without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split heavily by party: 238 of 242 voting Republicans (98%) voted yes while 153 of 181 voting Democrats (85%) voted no, with 28 Democrats crossing over; the motion to recommit fell entirely along party lines (180-237) [S7][S8].

industries.note: The bill would hand TransCanada a legislatively mandated approval of its cross-border pipeline and waive further environmental review, insulating the project from the permitting process and multi-court litigation other projects face. Spill and land-use risks would fall on the public along the route.

A new route to Gulf Coast refineries would expand the market for oil sands crude. The bill would also have kept oil sands products outside the same Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund treatment as conventional crude, a difference Democrats tried and failed to remove.
